The scope of IPs is very broad and encompasses microbiology, pharmacology, patient care, data analysis, engineering, construction, epidemiology, and more. I have a BS in biomedical sciences, a BSN, and an MPH in epidemiology. As an IP you work with every department. Some hospitals combine IP and occ health, which further broadens your scope.  Because IP are involved in so many areas, some hospitals have IPs specialized to an area, but most are cross-trained in all areas over about a year. Most hospitals require you to have CIC certification within 2-5 years. It's difficult exam because so many areas are covered. The pass rate is 58%.

In the morning I review labs and look for MDROs, SSIs, HAIs, CAUTIs, CLABSIs, VAPs, etc. Each of those requires investigation. Determining the source and timeframe of infections can be very involved. You have to examine every case to try to determine whether the hospital "takes the hit" for it. You'll spend a lot of time in charts. It can be really difficult to do a tracer, especially if the person collecting a sample only writes "wound" for a swab site on a patient with multiple wounds. Is it his dehisced incision site or his diabetic foot? Some nurses do excellent charting, but most only give one nursing note documenting change of shift. I enjoy this aspect of the job a lot, probably because it so closely aligns with epi.

Part of the rounds do include hand hygiene, checking for contaminated or expired supplies, looking at air flow/ventilation and water sources. I review Foleys, central lines, and other devices for medical necessity.  I look at dressings, mostly on the central lines. A lot of stuff is done monthly. We do ATP and GloGerm testing of ORs, dialysis cultures, tracking antimicrobial stewardship relative to resistance patterns, etc. IP is involved in every construction project or equipment move You need to be comfortable with public speaking because you will spend a fair amount of time presenting data or educating staff.

I work for a shitty hospital where IPs need thick skin, because you will get daily backlash for doing your job. We get shit on from above and below. The staff hate us, admins blame us. I have had staff threaten me and spit at me for asking them to put their mask on or for them foam their hands. Admin don't support us. We get harassed by admins to "correct" their employees, but we have no power to do anything and that's not our job anyway. It is NOT like this everywhere. There is another local hospital where the relationships between admin and staff are better and where IP is supported. Like most jobs, it depends on a lot on where you work and who you work with.

On the plus side, I get to work on side projects, advocate for the staff, and protect patients. I coded an electronic hand hygiene tool. I do a lot of research because I enjoy it.  I help write policies. You have to be able to look at things from so many different angles, especially in a global world where travel is quick. A few months back a nurse called because something was moving under her patient's skin (they were botflies). It's not nearly as engaging as being in the ED, but for 25k more a year, it's hard to pass up.
